rules.statement: Normalize a password to Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC), not NFKC or NFKD, before judging it against a policy, hashing it or verifying it.
rules.why: Devices and input methods produce different code-point sequences for the same visible text, so hashing the bytes as submitted turns one password into several. NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.1.1.2 and RFC 8265 name NFC, and the compatibility forms merge passwords that look different.
rules.check: Look for password hashing, verification or policy code that works on the raw submitted string or bytes without NFC normalization, or that uses NormalizationForm.FormKC or FormKD.

rules.statement: A password policy normalizes the password to NFC first, then counts Unicode code points (not UTF-16 chars) of the NFC form against the minimum and maximum length, then checks blocklists with the NFC form, in that order.
rules.why: The length checked must be the length of what gets hashed, and a decomposed spelling must not get past a blocklist that lists the composed spelling.
rules.check: Look for password length checks that use string.Length or count the submitted form, or blocklist lookups made before normalization or with the un-normalized password.

rules.statement: Do NFC normalization of a password inside the password hasher or policy itself, and have callers and stores pass the password as submitted instead of normalizing it themselves.
rules.why: The hasher owns what it hashes, so every store that uses it gets the same form, and only the hasher can fall back to verifying a stored hash of the submitted form. Normalizing in each caller repeats code and breaks that fallback.
rules.check: Look for callers, stores or endpoints that call Normalize() on a password before passing it to the hasher or policy.

rules.statement: Hold the decoded and re-encoded intermediate copies of a password in sensitive buffers rented from a pinned, zeroing secure pool, and dispose them as soon as they have been used.
rules.why: Password plaintext must not stay in unpinned, unzeroed managed memory.
rules.check: Look for password decode/normalize/encode steps that allocate plain strings or arrays, or that use rentals which are not sensitive or are not disposed right away.

rules.statement: When password bytes are not valid UTF-8, hash and verify them as they are instead of throwing or rejecting them.
rules.why: Invalid UTF-8 spells no text that could be normalized.
rules.check: Look for a password hasher that throws on, or rejects, input that fails UTF-8 decoding.

rules.statement: When verifying a password, verify the NFC form first. If that fails and the NFC form differs from the submitted form, verify the submitted form, report a match as PasswordVerificationResult.SuccessRehashNeeded, and replace the stored hash with the hash of the NFC form.
rules.why: Hashes already stored from un-normalized passwords must keep working and be migrated to the NFC form.
rules.check: Look for verification that only tries one form, that returns plain Success for a match on the submitted form, or that rehashes using the submitted form.

rules.statement: Do not add a format marker to password hashes to skip the legacy-form fallback. Run the fallback for every hash so that verification time does not depend on the format of the stored hash.
rules.why: A timing difference would reveal the format of an account's hash, and ASP.NET Core Identity hashes have no room for a marker.
rules.check: Look for version or format flags on password hashes that switch verification paths, or for the fallback being skipped under conditions tied to the stored hash.

rules.statement: In an ASP.NET Core Identity adapter that sets or checks passwords for the server, hash with UserManager<TUser>.PasswordHasher and store the hash through IUserPasswordStore<TUser>, throwing NotSupportedException when the user store does not implement it. Never call CreateAsync(user, password), ResetPasswordAsync, GeneratePasswordResetTokenAsync, AddPasswordAsync, ChangePasswordAsync or CheckPasswordAsync.
rules.why: Those UserManager methods run IPasswordValidator<TUser> composition rules, which NIST forbids, and those rules refuse passwords the policy accepts, which produced 500 responses. Bypassing them leaves the host's own pages and their validators unchanged.
rules.check: Look for server code paths that call the listed UserManager password methods, or that remove or override the host's IPasswordValidator registrations instead.

rules.statement: When the stored hash is replaced only to migrate the format of the same credential, keep the security stamp and ignore a refused update. When a password is actually reset, rotate the security stamp (for example with UpdateSecurityStampAsync).
rules.why: A rehash does not change the credential, and the old hash still verifies if the update fails. A reset is a new credential, so existing sessions must be invalidated.
rules.check: Look for rehash-on-verify paths that rotate the security stamp or fail the sign-in when the update is refused, and for password-reset paths that leave the security stamp unchanged.
